To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) IgG4-RDs affecting the cardiovascular system may be associated with IRF, (ii) IRF is frequently accompanied by increased serum concentrations of IgG4, (iii) IRF may represent a “forme fruste” of IgG4-related periaortitis, and (iv) the presence of IgG4 plasma cell infiltration in aortic and periaortic locations should not be considered a diagnostic criterion of IgG4- related periaortitis.

(1) IRF is a fibro-inflamatory disorder included in the “chronic peraortitis spectrum” which, according to the current diagnostic criteria, can be included in the IgG4-RDS spectrum; (2) IRF can be associated with other systemic manifestations of IgG4-related disease, and (3) IRF can develop in the setting of an IgG4-related vasculitis, a condition which has not been previously reported.

(1) the prevalence of IgG4 plasma cell infiltration in the aortic wall and its branches of patients with IRF is similar to that reported in other IgG4-RDs; and (2) serum IgG4 levels are significantly higher in patients with IgG4-related aortic disease than in those with idiopathic chronic periaortitis.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of IRF cases in which IgG4-RDs are present.
the following questions: (1) what are the clinical features, diagnostic criteria, and treatment of IgG4-related cardiovascular diseases (IgG-4-RD CV)?
the study of a case of IRF with histopathologic findings suggestive of IgG4-related disease.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

IgG4-RS can be a cause of chronic periaortitis (IRF) and, in this setting, the presence of IgG4 plasma cell-rich inflammatory infiltrate in the periaortic tissue is not a mandatory requirement for its diagnosis [1].
IRF, a disease of unknown etiology, can be included in the spectrum IgG4-Rd [16].
, although IgG4-RS has been reported in the literature in a number of cases with aortic and coronary involvements, the real prevalence of this disease in the cardiovascular system is still unknown.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
IgG4-RDS is a systemic disorder whose pathogenesis is not yet fully understood and that its clinical manifestations can be quite variable.
the histopathologic findings of IRF and IgG4-RDS overlap in some aspects.
, despite the fact that IgG4-RS has been reported as a cause of aortitis and IRF, its role in this clinical setting remains to be clarified.
The main takeaway from our work is that

, despite the increasing interest in the cardiovascular involvement in IgG4-RDs and the growing number of reports describing the histopathologic characteristics of the aortic lesions, a precise definition of the clinical and histopathologic features of the cardiovascular manifestations of IgG4-related disease is still lacking.
, although IRF is a rare disease, it is still underdiagnosed and, in some cases, it could be confused with IgG4-RS.

, despite the fact that the histopathology of IgG-4 related retroperitoneal lesions is similar to that of other systemic manifestations of the disease, the clinical presentation, course, and response to therapy of these patients are not always in line with those reported in the literature for other IgG4-RDs [1,16].
